extracted.intended_audience: fiction writers, creative-writing students, and authors thinking about conflict and tension in stories
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on identifying, classifying, and using different types of conflict in fiction and on quality criteria and anti-patterns for making conflict effective in a story.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foundational Distinction — External vs. Internal
rubrics_metrics.description: External conflict — protagonist vs. outside force; Internal conflict — psychological struggle within the protagonist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this primary classification to decide whether the source of struggle is outside the character (other people, society, nature, technology, supernatural forces) or inside (moral/psychological tension). Many stories combine both types.

rubrics_metrics.name: Person vs. Person
rubrics_metrics.description: Antagonist character (most common — Holmes vs. Moriarty).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conflict arises from another character whose aims oppose the protagonist. Make the antagonist active and plausible; use interpersonal stakes and conflicting goals to drive scenes and plot.

rubrics_metrics.name: Person vs. Society
rubrics_metrics.description: Individual against social/cultural systems (examples: 1984, The Handmaid's Tale).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conflict pits the protagonist against institutions, norms, laws, or cultural expectations. Show systemic pressures and how they constrain choices; use to explore political/social themes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Person vs. Nature
rubrics_metrics.description: Survival against natural forces (examples: The Old Man and the Sea, Into the Wild).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Nature functions as the antagonist — weather, environment, animals. Emphasize stakes of survival, isolation, and the protagonist's resourcefulness or limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Person vs. Technology
rubrics_metrics.description: Against machines/systems they made (examples: Frankenstein, 2001).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conflict with technological systems, AI, or human-made systems. Explore themes of control, unintended consequences, and human dependence on artifacts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Person vs. Supernatural
rubrics_metrics.description: Against gods, ghosts, fate (examples: Job, The Odyssey, Greek tragedies).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supernatural forces, divine will, or fate operate as antagonists. Clarify rules of the supernatural and the stakes; consider whether the force is literal or symbolic for thematic purposes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Person vs. Self
rubrics_metrics.description: Internal psychological/moral struggle (examples: Crime and Punishment, Hamlet).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inner conflict over beliefs, desires, guilt, identity, or decision-making. Show the inner stakes through thought, choice, and behavior; link inner turmoil to external actions for drama.

rubrics_metrics.name: Person vs. Fate / Destiny (Hybrid)
rubrics_metrics.description: Against predetermined outcomes; can be external (gods) or internal (resignation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This hybrid conflict blends external forces and inner acceptance/resistance. Use tension between agency and inevitability to explore themes of freedom, courage, or fatalism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stakes are real
rubrics_metrics.description: Protagonist could lose something important.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make consequences tangible and meaningful (life, relationships, reputation, values). Clear, high-stakes consequences make conflict emotionally engaging.

rubrics_metrics.name: Both sides have weight
rubrics_metrics.description: Antagonist isn't a strawman.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give the opposition believable motives, resources, and credibility. Avoid one-dimensional antagonists; show why their aims make sense from their perspective.

rubrics_metrics.name: External + internal interplay
rubrics_metrics.description: The outer fight forces inner reckoning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use external pressures to reveal and transform internal conflicts (and vice versa). Let external events create moral tests or growth opportunities for the protagonist.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conflict drives plot
rubrics_metrics.description: Events arise from conflict, not coincidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure plot developments follow logically from characters' opposing aims and choices. Avoid contrived coincidences; cause-and-effect rooted in conflict keeps narrative momentum.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resolution earned
rubrics_metrics.description: Outcome flows from character choice, not deus ex machina.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make sure endings arise from established character traits, decisions, or actions. Avoid sudden external fixes that undercut the story's emotional logic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theme tested by conflict
rubrics_metrics.description: The story's argument is stress‑tested by its conflicts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use conflict to probe the central thematic question(s). Show competing values in tension so the reader can see how the theme holds up under pressure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use multiple conflicts together
rubrics_metrics.description: The best stories use multiple conflicts (external + societal + internal) in interplay to generate depth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Layer person-vs-person, person-vs-society, and person-vs-self (for example) so conflicts echo and complicate one another, producing richer character arcs and thematic resonance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Failure mode — Conflict introduced too late
rubrics_metrics.description: Conflict introduced too late.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid delaying the presentation of central tensions until deep into the story; early and escalating conflict engages readers and sets stakes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Failure mode — Antagonist too weak
rubrics_metrics.description: Antagonist too weak (no real opposition).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A weak antagonist reduces suspense and makes outcomes feel inevitable; strengthen opposition or complicate the protagonist's path to keep tension credible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Failure mode — All external, no inner stakes
rubrics_metrics.description: All external, no inner stakes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stories that only present external obstacles can feel hollow; add internal stakes so outcomes matter to the character's identity or values.

rubrics_metrics.name: Failure mode — All inner, no dramatic events
rubrics_metrics.description: All inner, no dramatic events.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Purely internal conflict without external manifestation can lack dramatic momentum; externalize inner struggle through actions and consequences to create scenes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Failure mode — Conflict resolved by chance
rubrics_metrics.description: Conflict resolved by chance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid resolutions that depend on random events. Make resolutions the result of character choices or established plot dynamics to maintain plausibility and satisfaction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Failure mode — Conflict resolved off-page
rubrics_metrics.description: Conflict resolved by something off-page.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don't let important confrontations happen out of view; staging resolutions on-page preserves dramatic payoff and reader investment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Donald Maass's Micro-Conflict Principle
rubrics_metrics.description: Even within 'quiet' scenes, there should be small tensions — between characters, within character, between desire and obligation, between past and present. Tension on every page.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure micro-conflicts (minor disagreements, inner hesitations, unmet desires) populate scenes to sustain interest and reveal character; avoid completely tension-free pages.
